adversely affected by obesity. Obese individuals tend to marry mates with less education and from a lower socioeconomic class.
It is more difﬁcult for an obese person to ﬁnd a job or to be promoted once hired, so lower earnings and a lower socioeconomic
status are correlated with obesity. Obese employees are viewed as less competent, less productive, inactive, disorganized, and less
successful by employers, regardless of actual productivity.
The bias against obesity has been shown to begin in early childhood. Obese children are considered lazy, stupid, slow, and self-
indulgent by both children and adults. Because of these societal attitudes, many obese children and adolescents have lower levels of
self-esteem than do their nonobese counterparts
Economic Impact
In the USA, the direct cost of obesity has been estimated at almost 150 billion dollars per year. The indirect costs of early retirement
and increased risk for disability requiring ﬁnancial support are also considerable. Because obese people have more health problems,
health-care costs for the obese are higher than for lean individuals.
